items.title: Some quadratics never touch zero — and you can prove it in one step
items.claim: x^2 + 2x + 5: positive for every real x. The graph never reaches zero. You don't need calculus or graph-plotting — you can see this in one rearrangement.

options.text: Complete the square: x^2 + 2x + 5 = (x + 1)^2 + 4. The first term is non-negative; adding 4 means the whole expression is at least 4. Never zero
It cannot be proved without calculus

items.reveal:
For ax^2 + bx + c with a > 0, the discriminant b^2 - 4ac determines:
- Discriminant > 0: two real roots; graph crosses x-axis twice.
- Discriminant = 0: one repeated real root; graph touches x-axis.
- Discriminant < 0: no real roots; graph stays entirely above x-axis (if a > 0) or below (if a < 0).

x^2 + 2x + 5: a = 1, b = 2, c = 5. Discriminant = 4 - 20 = -16 < 0. No real roots.

Completing the square gives a stronger statement: the MINIMUM value of the quadratic. (x + 1)^2 + 4 has minimum 4 when x = -1. So x^2 + 2x + 5 is always at least 4.

General quadratic ax^2 + bx + c = a(x + b/(2a))^2 + (c - b^2/(4a)). Minimum value (for a > 0) is c - b^2/(4a) = -(b^2 - 4ac)/(4a) — same expression as the discriminant.

Applications:
- Optimisation: many minimisation problems reduce to completing the square.
- Inequality proofs: AM-GM and Cauchy-Schwarz often pivot on quadratic positivity.
- Definite matrices: a quadratic form x^T M x > 0 for all non-zero x means M is positive definite — central to optimisation and statistics.
items.why: Quadratics feel like they should always cross zero somewhere. Many don't. The discriminant settles which ones, and completing the square exposes the minimum directly — without calculus.

items.title: A 99% accurate medical test for a rare disease usually gives a false positive
items.claim: A test for a rare disease is 99% accurate (1% false positive rate, 1% false negative rate). The disease affects 1 in 10,000 people. You test positive. What's the chance you actually have the disease? Roughly 1%, not 99%.

options.text: Base rate matters. Out of 10,000 random people: ~1 truly has the disease (and tests positive); ~100 don't have it but test positive anyway (1% of 9999). Total positives ~101, true positives 1. So P(disease given positive) ≈ 1/101 ≈ 1%
False positives are impossible for accurate tests

items.reveal:
Bayes's theorem: P(disease | positive) = P(positive | disease) * P(disease) / P(positive).

P(positive | disease) = 0.99 (test sensitivity).
P(disease) = 0.0001 (base rate — the prevalence).
P(positive) = P(positive | disease) * P(disease) + P(positive | no disease) * P(no disease) = 0.99 * 0.0001 + 0.01 * 0.9999 ≈ 0.0001 + 0.01 = 0.0101.
P(disease | positive) = 0.99 * 0.0001 / 0.0101 ≈ 0.0098 = 0.98%.

The 'accuracy' of the test is misleading when the disease is rare. The vast majority of positives are FALSE positives, drawn from the much larger pool of healthy people.

Key insight: rare conditions produce rare true positives. Even excellent tests produce overwhelming numbers of false positives in screening contexts.

Real-world implications:
- Mass screening for rare cancers, HIV, etc., requires careful interpretation of positives.
- Drug tests at low real-prevalence give many false accusations.
- Airport security: very low base rate of terrorists; almost all positives are false alarms.
- Mammograms in the 40-49 age group: famous case of low base rate leading to controversy over screening recommendations.

Professionals routinely misinterpret. Gigerenzer's studies show many doctors get this wrong on similar problems. Communicating in 'natural frequencies' (1 in 10,000) rather than probabilities (0.0001) helps people reason correctly.
items.why: Test accuracy seems to translate directly to confidence in results. Bayes's theorem forces a different interpretation: when the condition is rare, even sensitive tests produce mostly false positives. Whole branches of medicine and public policy depend on getting this right.

items.title: The chain rule explains why a car's acceleration depends on both gear and rpm
items.claim: A car's speed (v) depends on engine rpm (omega) through the gear ratio. Engine rpm depends on time as the driver presses the throttle. The chain rule says dv/dt = (dv/d(omega)) * (d(omega)/dt). Acceleration is the product of two derivatives.
items.prompt: What's the chain rule's geometric meaning?

options.text: When y depends on u and u depends on t, a small change in t produces a small change in u (scaled by du/dt) which produces a small change in y (scaled by dy/du); chaining the scalings gives dy/dt = (dy/du)(du/dt)
It is wrong for vector quantities

items.reveal_title: The chain rule as composition of rates
items.reveal:
If y = f(u) and u = g(t), then y = f(g(t)). The chain rule: dy/dt = f'(g(t)) * g'(t) = (dy/du) * (du/dt).

Geometric intuition: a small Delta t produces a small Delta u (approximately (du/dt) * Delta t), which produces a small Delta y (approximately (dy/du) * Delta u). Combining: Delta y ≈ (dy/du)(du/dt) Delta t. Take the limit and you get the chain rule.

Physics examples:
- A particle's position depends on time. Its velocity depends on its position (e.g., in a velocity field). Acceleration = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v dv/dx. This is the Eulerian-Lagrangian connection in fluid mechanics.
- Optics: refractive index varies with position. The ray equation involves chain rules through the index.
- Thermodynamics: pressure depends on temperature and volume. Derivatives form a web of chain rules — Maxwell relations.

The chain rule is the BACKBONE of backpropagation in neural networks: gradients of a loss with respect to weights are computed via chain rules through layers of the network. Training deep neural networks is essentially repeated chain rule applications across millions of parameters.

When u or g has multiple components (vector-valued), the chain rule becomes the JACOBIAN rule — products of matrices of partial derivatives.
items.why: The chain rule looks like a notational identity. It's the fundamental principle of compositional change — appearing in physics, optimisation, neural networks, and any setting where one variable depends on another through an intermediate.
